name: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
title: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
answer: In the early grades, most general AI tools are not built for young children, so the adults in the building are the intended users. The largest benefit and the smallest risk sit with teacher preparation work, such as drafting stories, schedules and family notes. When a young child does use an AI tool, the school should be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching.

sections.body: This idea is about who actually holds the account when AI enters preschool through second grade. Most general AI tools are made for adults, and several of the common ones either exclude students entirely or let them in only through a school's own arrangement. That means the realistic first user in an early years setting is the teacher, not the child. The problem it solves is a mismatch between tools designed for general adult use and classrooms full of children who are years away from being able to use them independently. Naming the intended user up front keeps schools from handing young children accounts that were never meant for them.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, the text places teacher use at the centre. An early childhood teacher spends hours each week on work AI handles well, including writing short stories pitched at a child's level, making picture schedules, drafting notes to families, and turning scattered observations into clear summaries. Recovering even part of that time returns minutes to the teacher on the floor with children, and the text calls that trade the heart of the chapter. Where students are involved at all, the arrangements differ by tool: one educator tool offers no student accounts, another requires educator accounts to belong to adults with students using it only through a school's own setup, and a third lets teachers invite students but requires parental consent for those under 13. A preschooler or first grader is years away from the age line the guidance sets for independent conversations with generative AI.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one piece of external guidance rather than a study of outcomes: UNESCO recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI (Miao & Holmes, 2023). Everything else here rests on practice and on the account rules the tools themselves set, not on research findings about learning gains. The claim that teacher time savings translate into more minutes with children is presented as the chapter's reasoning, not as a measured result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by age and by supervision. Independent conversations with generative AI are not for young children under the guidance the text cites, and a preschooler or first grader sits well below that line. Where a tool does allow student access, the conditions are adult accounts, school-controlled setup, and parental consent for students under 13. The decision that stays with people is accountability: when a young child uses an AI tool, the school should be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching. Choosing whether to invite students at all, and obtaining consent, remain human decisions rather than tool defaults.
